Make five removable covers for the existing mattress.

Make five covers with two faces, four rectangular sides, a concealed #5 coil zip along one long side, and a small fabric pocket over the closed zip pull. Use the same cloth on both faces so you can turn the cushions over. Put your fitted sheet over the assembled bed.
This method hides the zip behind two fabric folds. You will see two lines of stitching alongside them. Use a standard zipper foot for this construction. The pocket in these steps hides the zip pull.

Check the mattress you already own
Remove its removable outer cover. Measure the bare foam's usable length, width and thickness with it lying flat and uncompressed. Record those three measurements here. You need a usable rectangle
for the current design. Check both ends and the middle for thickness: the CAD currently assumes

Keep any bonded foam layers together while measuring. If the usable rectangle is smaller, or the thickness differs, update the CAD and these cut dimensions before cutting. Keep the mattress intact until the bench dimensions have passed your physical mock-up check.

Compare each sample against your arm and through your fitted sheet. Check the weave for gaps or loose loops, then sew two layers, four layers, and the zip-and-pocket assembly on the machine you will use. Check for skipped stitches, puckering and a seam you can pull apart. Use the sample-washing steps in 2.1.8.

Machine access and beginner tuition in Wellington
. They welcome complete beginners and provide sewing machines. The last Monday of each month is for community projects. The website leaves the fee and machine models unspecified.
. A private lesson using their machine costs
. Their first-time-sewer pathway starts with a private lesson, followed by project sessions:
. They currently publish a lesson waitlist. Weekday machine hire costs
; hire covers machine support, while the lesson and project sessions include sewing tuition.

For your first lesson, the useful skills are bobbin winding and insertion, needle threading, speed control, a straight 15 mm seam, reverse stitching, changing to the zipper foot, zigzagging an edge and sewing the concealed zip. Use your actual fabric and zip for the layer checks. Neither venue publishes enough equipment detail to confirm that its machines will sew your chosen fabric's pocket and corner seams.

For these covers, the machine needs straight stitch, reverse, zigzag and a standard zipper foot. Both models below have foot-pedal speed control. Electronic stitch selection and a separate speed limiter add convenience; the cover construction uses basic stitches.
Mechanical stitch controls. Includes zipper foot, adjustable presser-foot pressure and extra foot lift. Pressure adjustment lets you change how firmly the foot holds the cloth against the feed teeth.

Electronic stitch selection, seven-point feed teeth and a foot-levelling button for thickness changes. Its separate speed limit and needle-position button are convenience features. The NZ listing leaves zipper-foot supply and pressure adjustment unclear.

The Singer has a lower advertised price and a documented pressure adjustment. Neither listing establishes which machine will feed your chosen upholstery layers better. Compare a two-layer seam, the zip attachment and the folded pocket/corner stack; check for skipped stitches, uneven feeding and a stalled or deflected needle. That comparison matters more here than maximum speed or the number of decorative stitches. Record the machine, needle and settings that work with the selected fabric.
Wash a sample and check your tape and markings

Use the chosen fabric's care instructions. Measure a swatch, wash and dry it using those settings, and measure it again. Check its feel and finish. Wash and dry the cover fabric before cutting if the supplier approves that process. Measure its usable width afterwards.

Mark and cut the first cover's fabric pieces
Lay the cloth flat with its wrong side up. Mark the first cover's rectangles from the cut table using a ruler and square. Label each piece
Inside each structural raw edge, draw a line

from that edge. Mark the intersections at the corners and mark the midpoint of each edge. Cut along the outer rectangle with fabric scissors. Keep the inner lines for sewing. On the pocket, mark the 80 mm direction as running along the zip.
Zigzag the cut edges on the sewing machine
Fit the ordinary zigzag foot. On a scrap of your cloth, set
zigzag width 3 mm and length 2 mm

. Guide it so the right-hand swing passes just beyond the raw edge and the left-hand swing catches the cloth. Sew 100 mm and inspect it. If the edge curls, reduce the upper-thread tension a little and repeat on the scrap; retain the setting that leaves it flat.

Zigzag around each cut panel, keeping its marked 15 mm stitch lines intact. After cutting the folded zip seam open in the next step, zigzag each of its two new raw edges separately. Keep those allowances apart as you sew them.

Hold the pocket in place for the cushion seams

Tape the pocket's three raw edges inside the panel's 15 mm seam allowances. Leave the hemmed mouth free so you can reach the pull. The side, top and bottom seams will secure those three edges while you assemble the cover.
Open and close the zip and tuck the pull under the pocket. Its depth after the corner seam will be about

Sew the four sides into a ring

Arrange solid long side, short side 1, zip side and short side 2 around the top face. Put neighbouring ends right sides together. Align their top and bottom raw edges. On the right-backrest cover, each panel is
15 mm from the short raw end
. Backstitch at both ends. Join all four corners, closing the ring. Finger-press those seam allowances apart. Keep their unsewn top and bottom ends free for attaching the faces.
Tape the top face to the side ring
Put the top face right side up. Place the ring against its edges with right sides together. Match the piece labels, edge midpoints and four marked 15 mm corner intersections.

Tape one edge at a time inside the allowance. At each corner, fold the neighbouring side's loose allowance away from the edge you are about to sew. Match the marked seam intersections. If the lengths differ, check the cut sizes and corner marks before stitching.
Sew the top face to the ring
Fit the ordinary foot and set straight stitch to
, starting at one marked corner intersection and ending at the next. Backstitch two or three stitches at the beginning and end. Support the loose fabric on the table and let the machine feed it.

At each corner, stop and reposition the loose allowances before sewing the next edge. Keep the adjacent side out from under the needle. Check that the two stitch lines meet at the same intersection and leave no corner hole. Inspect the first corner for trapped cloth and a gap between the stitch lines before sewing the other three.
Open the zip and attach the bottom face
Open the zip at least halfway. Match the bottom face's labels to the top, then tape it to the ring, right sides together. Match the edge midpoints and marked corner intersections.
, using the same corner-to-corner sequence as the top. Keep the opposite face and loose side fabric out of each seam. Leave the zip open so you can turn the cover through it.
Turn the cover right side out

Inspect the inside seams for missed layers and corner holes. Repair those seams before turning the cover. Reach through the zip and pull the cloth through. Push out the corners with your fingers or the rounded end of a smooth wooden spoon.
Open and close the zip. Check you can reach its pull under the pocket. Remove loose threads and visible tape. Keep the corner allowances intact for the first fitting.

Open the zip to its stops. Compress the right-backrest foam with your hands and feed it through the opening. Work the cover over the far corners, then over the near corners. Move the fabric over the foam a little at a time. Keep the foam's bonded layers aligned.

If the cloth grips the foam, wrap the foam in a clean thin plastic sheet with one end left accessible at the zip. Slide the cover over it, then pull the plastic out. Smooth the foam into the corners with flat hands.
Check this cover before making the other four

Compress the foam by hand to bring the zip sides together, then close the zip. Check for a flat foam block, filled corners, smooth faces and seams sitting at the edges. Remove and refit the cover once.
If the zip needs force or the foam bows, check your actual foam measurements and 15 mm seams. If those match, reduce the 10 mm fit deduction: try
if the foam barely compresses. A shallower seam can add room, but it also leaves less cloth beside the stitches. Check that alteration with the tutor before recutting the panel.

If the cloth bags, check for stretched fabric or seams shallower than 15 mm. Record the correction and revise all five cut-list rows before cutting more. Keep the successful first cover beside you while sewing the remaining four.
Fit all five cushions in the van
Arrange the pieces as seats and backrests, then make the
bed using the layout in 2.1.5. Put on your fitted sheet. Lie across the joins and sit on each seat. Check that you can lift the seats, reach the zips and remove the covers.

Use the slatted bed base already in the design. Lift the cushions after sleeping and let the undersides dry before packing bedding against them. Check the underside for dampness during the first few nights;
explains the need for airflow under foam.
Record the pattern and washing settings

Record each cushion's actual foam dimensions, final fit deduction, cut pieces, zip position, needle, machine model and stitch settings. Keep the fabric care instructions and a labelled scrap with this guide.

Remove the foam before washing the covers. Use the settings checked on your sample and dry the cover before refitting it. Update 2.2 with the cloth and zip quantities you used and the amounts you paid.

What this means for your five cushions
Your cut-up mattress and convertible benches match the first two van builds.
Washable cotton duck/drill/canvas and washable cotton/polyester upholstery fabric
have direct owner examples for this job. The boat reports add service-history evidence for cotton drill, polycotton and ordinary upholstery cloth.

For the current NZ comparison, the cotton duck and canvas rows match a documented fabric family. The Moreland polyester rows match the broader upholstery route, but still lack washing instructions. None of the owner reports used those exact NZ products. The cotton listings also leave stain resistance unverified.

A cotton cover will need laundering after spills that soak into it. The fitted sheet covers the bed at night; the covers remain exposed when you use the benches. Keep both washing and seat-surface feel in the comparison. The owner's choice of a fibre alone cannot establish a particular cloth's stain resistance or seam strength.

Vinyl is another documented route, including the NZ build above. Its construction and cleaning differ from the woven, washable covers in the current sewing steps. It remains an example in this research, with no added purchase row.
